Let’s talk gameplay: you walk. That’s it. You walk. You don’t even swing your weapon. The game does that for you. Because apparently the developers saw how little effort gamers were putting into life and said, “Let’s meet them halfway.” It's like a bullet hell shooter got drunk and passed out on a CRT monitor from 1993, and somehow, it’s art.
And oh, the dopamine. Every pixel explosion, every shiny gem, every upgrade — it’s like your brain is getting suckled by an arcade machine from a timeline where Castlevania went completely feral. Level up every 7 seconds.
The soundtrack? Banger. Absolute banger. I’ve started hearing “Revenant” in the background while doing dishes. My dishwasher has a kill combo. I don’t even have a dishwasher.
The characters? Oh, the deep, rich, emotionally resonant lore of “Guy With Axe” and “Skeleton With Gun.” There are approximately 947 playable characters and they all boil down to: “Hits stuff good.” Thank God. If I wanted emotional arcs, I’d rewatch Breaking Bad. I’m here to walk in a circle while deleting legions of undead like a Roomba with war crimes.
And don’t get me started on the items. Laurel? Yes, please, give me a shield so I can feel something. Clock Lancet? The game equivalent of putting the entire universe on hold while you decide whether to eat string cheese. The real star though? Garlic. You get Garlic, and you become a stinky god of rot and glory. You ever walked into a room so pungent you kill Death itself? You will.
Eventually, the game rewards you with a mode called Endless. Bold of them to assume I haven’t already been living in that mode since the day I installed it.
And yet. And yet. I cannot stop. I am freebasing pixels. I am optimizing builds in my sleep. I see red XP gems in my dreams. My mouse hand has calcified into a permanent WASD claw, but my soul? My soul is radiant. Bathed in golden chests and the unholy light of duplicator rings.
10/10. Highly recommend. Don’t do this to yourself.

You finish up your meal and the wait staff brings you a huge piece of cheesecake that you didn't order.  You want to send it back, but again, you don't want to cause a scene, so you take the cheesecake. When the cheesecake hits your tongue, you realize you are not in love with your date. The check finally comes. Before looking at it you start doing the math in your head. This is an RPG Auto-battler enemy hell (bullet hell). You control the progression and pathing of your character, the game handles the actual combat, making for a near perfect synergy between game and gamer.

There are currently four main maps and then a bunch of specialty maps, one of which was almost definitely designed specifically to help you expedite your unlocks. Each has its own unique theme.

Unlocks are the progression system in this one, and it works. Accomplishing almost any unique task or reaching certain levels will unlock the next things in line. However, character unlocks have an additional cost in gold (acquired in game). Similarly, permanent character boosts can be unlocked and all characters receive the benefits of all unlocks. There are even more things to unlock veyond those, and everything not only feels practical, but have a noticeable affect on gameplay.

You'd think that it being an enemy (read: bullet) hell, and with an array of abilities at your disposal, the screen would fill up quickly, and it does, but somehow, the devs managed to make your avatar noticeable and trackable no matter how high the screen chaos gets.

Speaking of which, for lofi graphics, these are just flat out cool. Again, it just works. The soundtrack mirrors this, and you'll be able to switch between tracks as you please. Additionally, I find this is a great game to play while jamming your own tunes.

In my opinion, the value at 3 bucks and the huge amount of gameplay variety make this a no brainer. You get far less from any number of full priced AAA titles. AND...the game hasn't even concluded development yet. What other surprises do the devs have in store, I wonder?

“Long” version:
[u]Vampire Survivors[/u] is a 2D action roguelike developed and published by poncle where you must survive an endless onslaught of monsters, all while levelling up, unlocking new weapons/combos and rescuing new survivors.

After seeing it pop up on Steam while it was still in Early Access, I decided to give it a try, as I usually play games like this on my phone when I am bored. I am glad I gave it a chance; this game is awesome!
It is a very simple game that is very easy to get into but it also provides a decent challenge to keep things interesting.

[u]Vampire Survivors[/u] does not really have a story. You are dropped into a location and monsters start spawning in. I do not think there is much more to it. Honestly, it does not need a story, the gameplay is so good it carries the whole experience.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2825034547
Gameplay-wise, the game is very satisfying.
You start each round with no upgrades and you must defeat enemies and collect experience crystals dropped by monsters to level up. Every time this happens, you get to pick between 3 upgrades - these can grant you upgrades for weapons you are already using, brand new weapons or even passive items.
Some of the weapons/items can even create combos and unlock “ultimate” weapons that are usually much stronger.

There are several maps to choose from, but apart from a few of them being more “vertical” or “horizontal” when it comes to movement, they lack any real differences. Sure, one of them has a few corridors which lead to a bigger hall but it is nothing special. I did appreciate their visual variety, however.
The controls are very basic, as you do not have any direct control over the attacks you perform. You simply move around and, depending on the weapon, you either fire in whichever way you are facing, deal AoE damage or even fire random projectiles. Passive items will give you useful benefits such as more lingering effects on damage-over-time, faster cooldowns and even bigger projectiles and AoE.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2905183016
As mentioned before, the core gameplay is rather simple, but the sheer amount of customization is great. Each survivor comes with a different weapon and a passive effect and it is almost guaranteed that you will find a character that just “clicks” with the build/approach you want to take. I love characters which focus on AoE damage and that is what I went for in most runs; however, some areas were much harder for such builds and I had to tweak them or even go for a complete overhaul.

There are also special enemies (pretty much bosses) that will always drop a chest that contains 1-5 upgrades for your current weapons – these are super satisfying to open. Regular enemies have the change to drop random single-use items (like an orb that attracts every EXP crystal in the map) which are also incredibly useful.
While you will unlock a lot of items and characters at first, progress tends to hit a bit of a wall after 15 or so hours. I suggest you look at the unlock list so you can keep unlocking new things. It never gets “boring”, per se, but I found myself wondering why I played a couple of rounds and unlocked nothing.

When it comes to the graphics, [u]Vampire Survivors[/u] features a very charming, pixelated art-style. I really enjoyed it. Such simple graphics also allow it to run on not-so-modern rigs, so if that is something that is important to you, keep it in mind!

Sound is up next. The soundtrack is a banger – I found myself jamming to some sick tunes while laying waste to all sorts of evil monsters. Also, the little jingle that plays when you open a chest… Oh my… It is cathartic.
Sound effects are simple but also satisfying. Some weapons can score critical hits and those feel visceral and make you feel like a bada$$.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2905183273
The base game is inexpensive and has around 35-40 hours of content. That is a steal.
They also released some DLC which I reviewed [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/goodguynickpt/recommended/2230760?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url].

So yeah, I cannot recommend [u]Vampire Survivors[/u] enough. It is a simple game that is oddly satisfying and gives you a ton of bang for your buck. It is not the most balanced game, some builds are clearly better than others, but still, it is awesome!

Support the devs, get it! 😉

I watched a bunch of my friends playing this, and a handful of streamers.  Every time I watched I thought "what on earth could possibly be fun about this?  It looks so incredibly dull." In the first few seconds I realized that you don't even click or anything to attack.  It's all auto cast.  I generally hate that kind of thing, so we're off to an even worse start.

Then, about a min or to into that run, I got to something like my third or fourth level and suddenly hit a synergy between a couple of my skills and it mowed down a huge wave of enemies and carved a path for me to escape.  The dopamine hit was hard and surprising.  

Now, here I am, 8 hrs later, playing it on my deck any time I have a few minutes of spare time like a fucking addict.  It just keeps getting better and better.  It's the perfect balance between zone-out clicker and strategy, with an awesome between-game progression system that keeps me coming back over and over.  This is one of the best games I've played this year, and it was $3.  You really cannot go wrong.

Each character has their own unique weapon, and we can combine these weapons with a passive weapon, giving us an upgraded version of that weapon. During the game, we can have a maximum of 6 weapons, and we can upgrade each of them. However, there are... a lot of weapons to choose from throughout the game.

[h2][u]Overview[/u][/h2]
[i]Vampire Survivors[/i] is a reverse bullet hell that’s all about “numbers go up” and constantly unlocking new toys and levels through achievements. It is cheap, full of content, easy to learn and control and most importantly fun.

[h2][u]Gameplay [/u][/h2]
Simplicity is the name of the game, yet it’s rather addicting. The player moves around the map avoiding large hordes of monsters while a lone weapon auto-fires. That’s right, attacking is done automatically so the player only needs to focus on movement. Otherwise, they collect experience and chests in order to obtain more weapons and passive upgrades. With the correct combination, these weapons can evolve further into even more powerful weapons, a feature that’s key to future victory.

There is a large variety of weapons. There are close-range melee weapons, ranged, AOEs, single target barriers, etc. Upgrades include damage, additional projectiles, increasing area, reducing cooldown, etc. When the game really gets going, the screen is so full of colors and projectiles that the player can hardly see what is happening anymore. But the numbers keep going up.

After every run, the player will likely meet some new achievement getting yet new toys and levels to play around with. Which then lead to yet more unlockables. This game is just full of content and just when I think I am 100% done, a new patch or DLC comes out with even more content.

[h2][u] Characters[/u][/h2]
Along with the variety of weapons, there’s a large pool of characters to choose from as well. Characters have different starting weapons, stats, and have an ability unique to them. For example, one may gain a buff every X amount of levels, another may gain more experience faster, etc. Most importantly, they all look quite different and have some pretty cool designs. Vampire Survivors is a minimalist survival game built around one goal: stay alive long enough for your run to snowball into something ridiculous. It looks simple at first, but it’s engineered to keep you chasing the next “perfect” build.

You don’t aim in the usual way—most attacks happen automatically—so your main skill is positioning. You’re constantly deciding how to weave through crowds, when to circle for safe experience pickups, and when to abandon a greedy grab to avoid getting boxed in.

The heart of the game is the level-up draft. Every run asks you to commit to a plan: which weapons to take, which passive bonuses to pair with them, and how to prioritize upgrades so you hit key power spikes at the right time.

As you learn the item pool, the game becomes less random and more about strategy. Strong runs come from stacking synergies that complement each other—coverage, damage scaling, survivability—until the screen turns into a controlled mess of effects that deletes everything around you.

Progression between runs is fast and rewarding. You unlock new characters, stages, relics, and modifiers at a steady pace, and those unlocks meaningfully change what’s possible, so experimenting feels productive rather than wasted.

The pacing is one of its biggest strengths: early minutes are tense and scrappy, midgame tests whether your choices actually cohere, and late game is either a victory parade or a sudden failure if you didn’t build enough scaling. That arc makes even short sessions feel complete.

If you like quick runs, build crafting, and that “from weak to unstoppable” curve, Vampire Survivors is extremely hard to put down. If you want precise manual combat, complex movement tech, or narrative focus, it won’t scratch that itch—but as a pure loop of choices and escalation, it’s unusually sharp.

Ah, Vampire Survivors—a game so simple, so stupidly brilliant, that it bypassed my evil intellect entirely and struck me right in the dopamine gland. This... this cursed creation is a bullet-hell auto-attacking time vacuum disguised as an innocent retro game. I booted it up expecting a laugh. Four hours later, I was drooling in a trance, surrounded by 3,000 flashing numbers and wondering where my dignity had gone. NYEHHH!

Let’s be clear: this game looks like it was developed in a haunted microwave. The graphics are what happens when Castlevania and MS Paint have an awkward one-night stand. The music slaps so hard it woke up my minions from the dungeon. And the gameplay? It’s just moving. You move. That’s it. You don’t even attack. The weapons fire themselves while you strafe around like a caffeinated Roomba with divine power.

And yet… it is glorious.

You start as a weak little worm with a whip. You end as a screen-destroying celestial tornado of holy garlic and lightning books, melting legions of undead like you're the unholy blender of fate. At first, you struggle to survive a single minute. Later, you pity Death itself as it tries—and fails—to kill you for the fifth time while you’re AFK microwaving pizza rolls.

It is digital crack cocaine with pixel art. It has no right to be this good. The entire game is built on the premise: “What if numbers go up, and you feel good about it?” And it works. Every. Single. Time.

Balance? HA! Some weapons are useless garbage until they evolve into god-tier screen nuke cannons. Others are immediately busted. But who cares?! You’re too busy unlocking secret characters like a ghost dog with a flamethrower or a literal piece of furniture that kills stuff. Yes. A chair. That kills.

You want story? No. There is none. Stop asking. This is not for your brain. This is for your lizard brain. The part of you that shrieks in delight when your character gets three chests in a row and turns into a walking disco apocalypse. This game has zero plot, infinite gameplay, and endless regret when you realize it’s 3AM and you’re STILL TRYING TO UNLOCK QUEEN SIGMA.

And the best part? It costs five dollars. Five. Dollars. Diablo 4 sold you a trash fire at seventy bucks with a battle pass for armor dyes. This game sold you a lifetime supply of chaos, serotonin, and existential reflection for the cost of a sad sandwich. The only thing Vampire Survivors lacks is the ability to physically inject itself into your bloodstream. Which I’m sure is in a patch.

Final Verdict: 💀💀💀💀💀 (5 out of 5 Skulls)

Nice game to turn off your brain and forget about life. It requires zero execution skills, since all you do is move your character around and choose the equipment your character is going to equip/upgrade, and even though there are maps (at least for now) that require a little bit of planning, it all bow down to choosing a specific set of equipment to practically guarantee your victory, even though nowadays everything works. 

It may sounds like a negative aspect of the game, but something like Vampire Survivors doesn't need complex combat system to be fun. As simple as it is, it offers tons of fun and it's always great to see waves and waves of foes being obliterated and seeing your screen (and GPU) go crazy with so many visual effects from your weapons.

Be careful tho. Even though each run only has 30 minute duration, once you start and get the hang of it, it's hard to put it down. You'll see hours going by without knowing how haha.

And hey, it's cheap as hell and the devs are super active, always bringing new updates periodically. 
Gotta love when a indie dev shows WAY more support for their game than a AAA studio. It's the perfect reason to support this game and its devs.
